description: Waves and Sound: transverse vs longitudinal, speed of sound in media, resonance/standing waves, Doppler effect formula, intensity level (dB), ultrasound applications, musical note frequency.

questions.stem: Sound waves are classified as longitudinal waves because:

options.option_text: The particles of the medium vibrate parallel to the direction of wave propagation
The particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of propagation — that is a transverse wave
Sound can travel through vacuum by oscillating its own field lines instead
Sound waves carry energy without displacing any medium particles at all

questions.explanation: LONGITUDINAL WAVE: particle displacement is PARALLEL to wave propagation direction. Creates compressions (high pressure) and rarefactions (low pressure). SOUND: a mechanical, longitudinal wave — requires a medium (solid, liquid, gas). TRANSVERSE WAVE: particle displacement is PERPENDICULAR. Examples: light (EM), water surface waves, waves on a string. SOUND IN MEDIA SPEED: solid > liquid > gas (molecules closer → faster). Speed of sound in air at 0°C ≈ 331 m/s; at 20°C ≈ 343 m/s. KEY: Sound CANNOT travel in vacuum (no medium); light CAN (EM wave, no medium needed). PYQ FREQUENCY: longitudinal vs transverse in SSC CGL, IBPS PO physics — standard 1-mark question.

questions.stem: The Doppler effect states that when a sound source moves toward a stationary observer, the observed frequency:

options.option_text: Increases — the wavefronts are compressed, raising the perceived frequency (pitch)
Decreases — this is what happens when the source moves AWAY from the observer
Remains unchanged — the frequency only changes if the observer moves, not the source
Becomes zero — the Doppler effect never reduces frequency to zero for subsonic sources

questions.explanation: DOPPLER EFFECT: apparent change in frequency due to relative motion of source and observer. SOURCE MOVES TOWARD OBSERVER: wavefronts pile up → shorter wavelength → higher frequency (higher pitch). SOURCE MOVES AWAY: wavefronts spread out → longer wavelength → lower frequency (lower pitch). FORMULA: f_obs = f_s × (v ± v_obs)/(v ∓ v_s). CLASSIC EXAMPLE: train horn pitch rises as it approaches, drops as it passes (the 'whoosh' effect). APPLICATIONS: (1) RADAR speed guns (police). (2) SONAR (submarines). (3) Echocardiogram (blood flow). (4) Astronomical redshift/blueshift (galaxies moving away/toward us). PYQ FREQUENCY: Doppler effect concept in UPSC, SSC CGL, IBPS PO — 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: The intensity level of a sound increases from 40 dB to 70 dB. By what factor does the actual intensity (in W/m²) increase?

options.option_text: 1000 times — every 10 dB corresponds to a factor of 10 in intensity; 30 dB = 10³
30 times — incorrectly treats dB as a linear scale instead of logarithmic
100 times — corresponds to only a 20 dB increase, not 30 dB (not this)
10 times — only a single 10 dB step; total increase here is 30 dB = three steps

questions.explanation: DECIBEL (dB): logarithmic scale. β = 10 log₁₀(I/I₀). Every 10 dB increase = 10× intensity. CHANGE: 70 − 40 = 30 dB. Number of 10-dB steps = 3. Intensity multiplier = 10³ = 1000. REFERENCE LEVEL: I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m² (threshold of hearing). EXAMPLES: 0 dB = threshold of hearing; 30 dB = whisper; 60 dB = conversation; 90 dB = lawnmower; 120 dB = pain threshold. SOUND PERCEPTION: human ear perceives a 10 dB increase as approximately 2× LOUDER (not 10×) — loudness perception is also logarithmic but different from intensity. PYQ: dB calculation in SSC CGL/UPSC Prelims physics — 1× per 2 cycles.

questions.stem: A closed organ pipe of length L resonates at its fundamental frequency. An open organ pipe also resonates at the same fundamental frequency. What is the length of the open pipe?

options.option_text: 2L — open pipe fundamental = v/2L; closed pipe fundamental = v/4L; equating gives open L = 2×closed L
L — same length only works if both pipe types had the same boundary conditions
L/2 — this is the closed pipe being half the open pipe, which inverts the relationship
4L — this over-doubles the required length for matching the fundamental (not this)

questions.explanation: OPEN PIPE: antinodes at both ends. Fundamental f = v/(2L). CLOSED PIPE: node at closed end, antinode at open end. Fundamental f = v/(4L). EQUATE: v/(4L_closed) = v/(2L_open) → L_open = 2 × L_closed = 2L. OVERTONES: open pipe produces all harmonics (n=1,2,3,...); closed pipe produces only ODD harmonics (n=1,3,5,...). MUSICAL APPLICATION: the fact that open pipes produce a richer tone (more harmonics) explains why open flutes sound fuller than stopped (closed) ones. PYQ: open vs closed pipe length comparison in IBPS PO physics section.

questions.stem: Ultrasound frequencies are defined as those above the human audible range. What is the approximate upper limit of human hearing, and in which medical application is ultrasound most widely used?

options.option_text: 20,000 Hz (20 kHz); sonography (imaging internal organs, monitoring foetal development)
2,000 Hz; X-ray imaging — X-rays are electromagnetic, not sound waves
200,000 Hz; MRI scanning — MRI uses magnetic fields and radio waves, not sound
20 Hz; ECG monitoring — ECG records electrical heart activity, not acoustic waves

questions.explanation: AUDIBLE RANGE: 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz) for humans. INFRASOUND: below 20 Hz (elephants, earthquakes). ULTRASOUND: above 20 kHz. MEDICAL APPLICATIONS: (1) SONOGRAPHY/ULTRASONOGRAPHY: 1–20 MHz; images soft tissues, organs, foetus. (2) ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY: heart imaging. (3) Lithotripsy: breaking kidney stones. (4) Phacoemulsification: cataract surgery. INDUSTRIAL USE: ultrasonic cleaning, flaw detection in metals (NDT). BATS/DOLPHINS: 20–200 kHz echolocation. PYQ FREQUENCY: ultrasound frequency range + medical use in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, UPSC — 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: Beats are heard when two tuning forks vibrate simultaneously. The number of beats per second equals:

options.option_text: The difference between their frequencies — beats = |f₁ − f₂|
The sum of their frequencies — the sum gives the carrier frequency, not the beat frequency
The average of their two frequencies — the average is the mean pitch heard, not the beat rate
The product divided by the sum — that formula applies to resistors in parallel, not to beats

questions.explanation: BEATS: when two sound waves of slightly different frequencies f₁ and f₂ interfere, they alternately reinforce and cancel. BEAT FREQUENCY = |f₁ − f₂|. AUDIBLE BEATS: perceptible when |f₁ − f₂| ≤ ~10 Hz (above that, we hear two distinct tones). APPLICATION: musicians use beats to tune instruments — when beats disappear (frequency = 0), strings are in unison. PHYSICS LINK: beats are a form of amplitude modulation. PYQ: fork tuning/beat frequency calculation in IBPS PO quantitative/physics hybrid — 1× per 2 years.

questions.stem: A bat emits a sound pulse at 50,000 Hz and the echo returns at 51,000 Hz. What does this tell us about the insect being hunted?

options.option_text: The insect is moving toward the bat — returning echo at higher frequency indicates approach (Doppler blueshift)
The insect is stationary — a stationary reflector would return exactly the same 50,000 Hz
The insect is moving away — that would return a lower frequency (Doppler redshift) (not this)
The echo indicates the insect has hard wings — wing hardness affects amplitude, not frequency

questions.explanation: DOPPLER ECHOLOCATION: bat emits 50 kHz; echo returns at 51 kHz (higher). Higher frequency echo = object APPROACHING the bat (or bat approaching object). DOUBLE DOPPLER: both bat moving and insect moving contribute to the frequency shift. FREQUENCY SHIFT DIRECTION: toward = higher (blueshift); away = lower (redshift). BATS' PRECISION: horseshoe bats can detect frequency shifts of 83 Hz at 83 kHz (0.1% change) — they can sense insect wing-beat frequency to identify prey species from echo modulation. UPSC/SSC ANGLE: Doppler + echolocation is a high-difficulty combination question linking two concepts.
